rag_matches.description: Dioecious shrub or tree, to 15 m tall; trunk slender or to 20 cm dbh and deeply invaginated; stems sericeous when very young, glabrate in age, with conspicuous leaf scars. Leaves somewhat clustered at apex of branchlets; stipules caducous, to 1 cm long, sericeous, leaving a conspicuous interpetiolar line of trichomes; petioles 6-14 mm long, sericeous to glabrate; blades ovate-elliptic to obovate-elliptic, abruptly short-acuminate, usually obtuse and ± decurrent onto petiole at base, 7-13(21) cm long, 3.5-8 (12) cm wide, glabrous or with sparse long trichomes on major veins below and tufts of trichomes in axils, the margins ciliate and ± revolute.

Tree, 4.5-35 m, the young twigs minutely adpressed-pubescent to glabrescent. Leaves with the petiole 0.5-1.2 cm; blade 10-30 X 3.5-12 cm, elliptical to oblong-elliptical, acute to obtuse or (rarely) subtruncate at the base, glabrous on the underside, without domatia or (rarely) with countable trichomes in the axils of the main veins, with (4)5-8 secondary veins on each side. Inflorescences [of Nectandra purpurea] 10-17 cm. Flowers with the tepals (1—)1.2—2(—2.4) mm. Fruits 1-1.5 cm, ellipsoidal; cup ca. 0.3 cm. Very wet and pluvial forest, 0-1550 m; Caribbean [vertical] Cords. of Guanacaste, Triarán and Central (E.B. La Selva), San Carlos and Tortuguero Plains, Low Talamanca, both [vertical] Cord. de Talamanca, [Pacific] vertical, S Coastal Range (Fila Cruces). Flowers [of Nectandra purpurea] May-Sept. [in Nicaragua, Bolivia] and [Venezuela], [in the] Guiana [region], [in] Brazil. (Grayum et al. 8898, MO) Nectandra purpurea is recognized by its leaf blades that dry relatively opaque on the adaxial side, with the secondary veins slightly elevated and interconnected, forming a submarginal vein and by its flowers with the tepals densely covered by brown or yellowish trichomes and (usually) with the staminodes conspicuously elevated. The cupules that dry light brown, ± puberulent, are also distinctive.

75 genera and about 1300 species, from the southern USA to Chile and Venezuela, Trinidad & Tobago, Guianas, Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay, Argentina, Antilles, Bahamas, tropical regions of the Old World (where less numerous and diverse); 19 genera and 75 species in Costa Rica. Trees, shrubs, or lianas, always perennial, pubescent with unicellular trichomes, usually medium-fixed or sub-medium-fixed; stipules usually present. Leaves simple, usually opposite (sometimes whorled), usually entire (lobed in some Stigmaphyllon species), primarily and pinnately veined, petiolate, often with large, multicellular glands on the petiole and/or the underside of the blade.

Tree, to 27 m tall and 40 cm dbh, glabrous to puberulent throughout; trunk ± involuted with many prominent horizontal wrinkles; outer bark thin; inner bark reddish; young stems very prominently lenticellate. Petioles margined; rachis margined to narrowly winged; leaflets in 2-5 (usually 4) pairs, narrowly ovate to lanceolate-elliptic or oblanceolate, acuminate, rounded to acute at base, slightly asymmetrical, the terminal pair 8-22 cm long, 2.5-8 cm wide. Spikes axillary in groups of 1-6; peduncles 1.5-3.5 cm long; rachis shorter than peduncle, very densely flowered, 0.5-3 cm long; bracts ca 5 mm long; flowers sessile; calyx 1-2(3) mm long, the lobes ca 0.5 mm long, blunt; corolla 4-8 mm long, the lobes blunt to acute, ca 1 mm long; stamens and style ca 1 cm long. Legumes flat, 10-22 cm long, (2)2.5-3 cm wide, ± glabrous, ± straight, the marginal ribs prominent, the fruits probably mature from July to October. Known only from Panama, from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone, Bocas del Toro, San Bias, Veraguas, Panama, and Darien, from premontane wet forest in Colon, Chiriqui, Code, and Panama.

Tree, to 27 m tall and 40 cm dbh, glabrous to puberulent throughout; trunk ± involuted with many prominent horizontal wrinkles; outer bark thin; inner bark reddish; young stems very prominently lenticellate. Petioles margined; rachis margined to narrowly winged; leaflets in 2-5 (usually 4) pairs, narrowly ovate to lanceolate-elliptic or oblanceolate, acuminate, rounded to acute at base, slightly asymmetrical, the terminal pair 8-22 cm long, 2.5-8 cm wide. Spikes axillary in groups of 1-6; peduncles 1.5-3.5 cm long; rachis shorter than peduncle, very densely flowered, 0.5-3 cm long; bracts ca 5 mm long; flowers sessile; calyx 1-2(3) mm long, the lobes ca 0.5 mm long, blunt; corolla 4-8 mm long, the lobes blunt to acute, ca 1 mm long; stamens and style ca 1 cm long. Legumes flat, 10-22 cm long, (2)2.5-3 cm wide, ± glabrous, ± straight, the marginal ribs prominent.

Tree, 3-8 (15) m tall, 5-35 cm dbh; wood yellow; stems weakly striate, brown or with a thin gray flaky crust, the leaf scars 3-sided, raised. Petioles 5-11 cm long, canaliculate, somewhat swollen at apex; blades ± oblong-elliptic, long-acuminate, obtuse to rounded at base, 10-30 cm long, 5-11 cm wide, glabrous, the midrib raised above. Panicles axillary and terminal, to ca 20 cm long; pedicels to 1.5 cm long; flowers ca 1.2 cm diam, conspicuous and sweetly scented; sepals 3, reflexed at anthesis, caducous; petals 6-12, white, blunt at apex; stamens numerous, unequal, exserted; anthers slightly bifid at apex; style 4-6 mm long; stigma shortly trilobate. Capsules 1-1.5 cm diam, covered with stiff bristles, dehiscing into 3 or 4 parts to expose seed; seed usually solitary, smooth, broadly ovate, ca 7 mm long, flattened on one side, gray-coated, with a shiny, bright red, lateral aril. [Croat 6097, 7753]. Locally abundant along some areas of the shore, especially on the southern side of the island; frequent in the forest. Flowers principally in the rainy season from May to October, rarely as early as April or as late as December. The fruits mature in the early dry season (January to March). Southern Mexico to northern South America. In Panama, known from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone, Chiriqui, Panama, and Darien, from premontane wet forest in Chiriqui and Panama, and from tropical wet forest in Colon.

Shrub or tree, 2-7(-20) m, the twigs grayish brown; stipules 0.2-0.25 cm. Opposite leaves, petiole 0.2-0.9 cm; blade to [unclear reference], scattered-1% [unclear reference]. Inflorescences with peduncle 0.4-8 cm, [unclear reference], [unclear reference]. Flowers with the articulated pedicel 1/7-1/2 of the base; sepals 1/3-1/2 the [unclear reference] coacuminate at the apex, 1-5-nerved; petals [unclear reference], extended laterally and apical-pubescent on the coast (especially distally); stamens [unclear reference], sparsely puberulent [unclear reference] (> the total length of the anther), subentire; style 1.75-2 mm. Fruits [unclear reference]; seeds 6-8 mm, puberulent. Very humid forest, often near water, 0-850 m; [unclear reference] of Agulcahs Pitilla and Talamanca, San Carlos Plains and [unclear reference]. Fl. mar.-may., nov.

Tree, to 15 m tall; branchlets ferruginous-puberulent when young, glabrous and prominently lenticellate in age. Petioles ribbed, 2-7 cm long; rachis winged; petiole and rachis sparsely ferruginous-pubescent; leaflets in 2-5 pairs, obovate to elliptic, acute to acuminate, obtuse to rounded at base, densely tomentose to puberulent especially on midrib and veins below, the terminal pair 11-26 cm long, 4.5-12 cm wide. Spikes usually axillary in groups of 1-3; peduncles usually sparsely tomentose, 1-5(6) cm long; floral rachis much shorter, 0.5-2(3) cm long; bracts to 12 mm long; calyx and corolla sparsely sericeous; calyx 6-13 (17) mm long, the lobes to 2 mm long; corolla 18-30 mm long, the lobes to 3 mm long; stamens and styles 4-5.5 cm long. Legumes tetragonal with prominently ribbed corners, 11-30 cm long, 1.5-3.5 cm wide, ca 1.5 cm thick, glabrate to densely pubescent. Common, at least along the shore. Seasonal behavior uncertain. Flowers from August to May, especially from November to February. Most fruits mature in the rainy season. An extremely variable species. Often planted for shade in coffee plantations. Mexico to Panama; West Indies. In Panama, known from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone, Bocas del Toro, San Bias, Code, Panama, and Darien and from premontane wet forest in Chiriqui (San Felix).

Guavita cansa-boca, Bribri, Guava, Guava del mono Tree, to 15 m tall; branchlets sparsely strigose when young, glabrate in age, minutely lenticellate, minutely ribbed below petioles (at least when dried). Leaves strigose throughout, especially on axis and midrib of leaflets; petiole and rachis terete to narrowly margined; leaflets in 2 or 3 pairs, lanceolate to elliptic, long-acuminate, acute to rounded at base, the terminal pair 9-18 cm long, 3.5-7.5 cm wide. Spikes axillary, in groups of 1-7; peduncle and rachis strigose; peduncles 2-4 cm long; rachis much shorter, 1-2.5 cm long; bracts subulate, to ± 2 mm long; calyx puberulent, 3-5 mm long, the lobes ± 1 mm long; corolla moderately sericeous, 5-9 mm long, the lobes to 2 mm long; stamens and style to ca 2 cm long. Legumes flat, to 16 cm long and 2 cm wide, minutely puberulent, the margins raised.

Locating an individual
It is mainly observed towards the Southern Boundary (LS), Quebrada El Salto, etc., in rolling or broken terrain.
Distribution
From Belize to Venezuela, the Guianas, Brazil, and Bolivia. In Costa Rica, it is widely distributed in the medium to low elevations of both slopes, in climates ranging from humid to very humid, although it prefers climates with marked seasonality; 0-700-800 m.
Habit
Trees, 15-35 m tall.
Trunk
Trunk with reddish-brown outer bark.
Bark
Outer bark reddish-brown, scaly, inner bark reddish with a pleasant mango scent; white or milky resinous sap.
Leaves
Odd-pinnate leaves, with 7-9 leaflets, elliptical, oblong, or oblong-lanceolate, 5-21 x 4-7.2 cm, apex acuminate to abruptly acuminate, base obtuse to asymmetric, generally glabrous; petiolules without evident pulvini, margin entire; petioles 4-14 cm long.
Flowers
Inflorescences are panicles, 3-15 cm long, axillary. Yellowish or greenish-yellow flowers (unisexual); calyx with 5 lobes, 1-1.5 mm long, cuculiform; petals (tubular corolla), with 5 lobes, 5-5.5 mm long; stamens 10, 1 mm long, filaments inserted at the base of the disc; annular disc with 10 lobes; ovary with 5 lobes, ovoid, with 5 locules; style 1, stigma with 5 lobes.
Fruits
Capsular and drupe-like fruits, 1.5-2.5 x 1.5 x 3 cm, ovoid or more or less turbinate, with 2-5 lobes, dehiscent by 4-5 valves, scarlet red inside, red to black when mature; pyrenes 3-5, 12-13 mm thick, white, the mesocarp (pseudoaril) reddish turning white upon exposure (dehiscence), fleshy, juicy, sweet, and edible.
Diagnosis
Characterized by being a large tree, the bark on mature trees is somewhat scaly, lenticellate, and the inner bark has a very particular and pleasant mango scent. At the vegetative level, it is sometimes confused with the genus Protium, although its leaves lack pulvinated petiolules and the turpentine aroma when crushed. Its fruits are distinctive for their peculiar turbinate shape.
Habitat
In the Forest; it is mainly observed towards the Southern Boundary (LS), Quebrada El Salto, etc., in rolling or broken terrain.
Phenology
Flowers observed in June and August; fruits in August and February.

Life Form: Tree, Shrub 10. Maquira Aubl. By C.C. Berg. Trees or shrubs, dioecious. Leaves alternate, distichous on lateral branches; blade leathery, margins entire, pinnate-veined; stipules not completely amplexicaul, free. Inflorescences on spurs in the axils of the leaves, unisexual, discoid-capitate, involucrate. Staminate inflorescences often several together, pedunculate; flowers not covered by the inner involucral bracts before anthesis, numerous; perianth 4-parted to 4-divided; stamens 4; pistillode absent. Pistillate inflorescences subsessile; flowers numerous; perianth 4-lobed; ovary adnate to the perianth; stigmas 2, tongue-shaped. Fruit-bearing perianth enlarged, fleshy, orange; fruits adnate to the perianth; seed large, without endosperm, cotyledons thick and equal. 4 spp. Tropical America.

Shrub, 1-1.8 m tall; stems and leaves glabrate. Stipules persistent, 3-5 mm long, bifid to near base, the lobes distant, acuminate; petioles 1-1.5 cm long; blades ± elliptic, acute to acuminate, cuneate at base, 10-16 (20) cm long, 4-6 cm wide, drying light green. Racemes short, terminal, usually to 1.5 cm long at anthesis, to 3 cm long in fruit; peduncles lacking or to 1.2 cm long; inflorescence branches, pedicels, and calyces with short, ± erect, sparse trichomes, the lowermost branches subtended by a distinct, oblong-elliptic bract ca 5 mm long; bracts green, ovate, 2-7 mm long, acute, foliate, persistent, subtending groups of 2-4(7) flowers, exceeding the flowers; flowers white, sessile, ca 3.5 mm long, the tube ca 2 mm long, the lobes oblong, to ca 1.5 mm long; filaments ca 0.5 mm long, affixed above the middle of the tube; anthers ca 1 mm long; style ca 4 mm long; stigmas 0.2 mm long. Berries ± globose, 3-4 mm diam, flattened laterally and somewhat grooved, glabrous or sparsely puberulent at least when immature; seeds 2, flat, with a deep groove on the inside surface, rounded and 4- or 5-grooved on the outside surface. Croat 11132. Apparently rare; found in the younger forest south of Fairchild Point and in the forest north of Barbour Trail. Flowers mostly from June to September, principally in July, rarely also in the dry season. The fruits mature from July to October, principally in August. In Panama, Psychotria brachybotrya is most easily confused with Psychotria involucrata Sw., a superfluous name for Psychotria officinalis (Aubl.) Sw. (Steyermark, 1972). Psychotria brachybotrya differs from Psychotria officinalis by having distinct bracts beneath the lower inflorescence branches and leaves that usually dry a lighter green. Psychotria brachybotrya usually occurs in drier areas than Psychotria officinalis, which occurs principally in premontane wet forest and tropical wet forest. Psychotria brachybotrya has also been confused with Psychotria furcata DC, but is distinguished from Psychotria furcata by its larger, lighter-colored leaves and green, rather than purple, inflorescence bracts. Psychotria brachybotrya is distributed from Panama to Colombia, Venezuela, the Guianas, Brazil, Peru, and Bolivia; Trinidad. In Panama, Psychotria brachybotrya is ecologically variable; known from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone, Bocas del Toro, Colon, Herrera, Panama, and Darien, from tropical dry forest in Panama, and from premontane wet forest in Colon, Panama, and Darien.
